sections.name: Hook
lines: g_hook
Your phone knows where you are, to within a few metres, using signals from space. And it never sends a single word back.
g_title
Here's how it pulls that off, in five steps.

sections.name: Clocks in space
lines: g_sats
Step one. About thirty GPS satellites circle the Earth, twenty thousand kilometres up, each going around twice a day.
g_clock
Each one carries atomic clocks, accurate to billionths of a second, and constantly broadcasts the time, and where it is.

sections.name: Timing the signal
lines: g_listen
Step two. Your phone only listens. It catches each signal and checks when it was sent.
g_delay
Radio travels at the speed of light, so a tiny delay reveals the distance. About seven hundredths of a second means roughly twenty thousand kilometres.

sections.name: Where spheres meet
lines: g_one
Step three. Knowing your distance from one satellite puts you somewhere on a giant sphere around it.
g_three
Add a second, and a third, and the spheres only cross in one spot on the ground. That's you.
g_four
A fourth satellite corrects your phone's own clock, which is far less precise. Just one millionth of a second off would put you three hundred metres out.

sections.name: Einstein's correction
lines: g_rel
Step four. Up there, weaker gravity makes time run slightly faster, while the satellites' speed slows it down a little.
g_fix
Overall, their clocks gain about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day. So engineers set them to tick slightly slow. Without that, GPS would drift by kilometres every day.

sections.name: Getting a fix
lines: g_block
Step five. Buildings and tunnels block or bounce the signals, which is why your dot wanders downtown.
g_assist
So phones get a head start. Nearby Wi-Fi networks and cell towers give a rough position first, and GPS sharpens it.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
Satellites send the time. Your phone times the delay, turns it into distances, and finds the one spot where they meet. With a little help from Einstein.
outro
Next time you follow that blue dot, remember the clocks in space. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
